plain_english: If you spend a lot of time with people — talking, drinking, or just hanging out — one of two things will happen. Either you'll become like them, or you'll change them to be like you. Think of it like putting a cold piece of charcoal next to a burning one. Either the cold charcoal will put out the hot one, or the hot charcoal will light the cold one. Since the risk is so high, be careful about getting close to ordinary people. Remember: you can't hang around someone covered in soot without getting soot on yourself.
original_excerpt: If a man has frequent intercourse with others either for talk, or drinking together, or generally for social purposes, he must either become like them, or change them to his own fashion. For if a man places a piece of quenched charcoal close to a piece that is burning, either the quenched charcoal will quench the other, or the burning charcoal will light that which is quenched. Since then the danger is so great, we must cautiously enter into such intimacies with those of the common sort, and remember that it is impossible that a man can keep company with one who is covered with soot without being partaker of the soot himself.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought with Caution to Enter into Familiar Intercourse with Men

plain_english: What will you do when someone talks about gladiators, horses, athletes, or worse — gossips about people? 'This person is bad, that person is good. This was done well, that was done badly.' What if they mock you, ridicule you, or act mean-spirited? Are any of us prepared like a musician who picks up a lute? As soon as he touches the strings, he knows which ones are out of tune and fixes them. Do you have the kind of power Socrates had? He could steer any conversation toward what mattered. How could you possibly have that skill? So of course you get swept along by whatever ordinary people are talking about.
original_excerpt: For what will you do if a man speaks about gladiators, about horses, about athletes, or what is worse about men? Such a person is bad, such a person is good; this was well done, this was done badly. Further, if he scoff, or ridicule, or show an ill-natured disposition? Is any man among us prepared like a lute-player when he takes a lute, so that as soon as he has touched the strings, he discovers which are discordant, and tunes the instrument? Such a power as Socrates had who in all his social intercourse could lead his companions to his own purpose? How should you have this power? It is therefore a necessary consequence that you are carried about by the common kind of people.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought with Caution to Enter into Familiar Intercourse with Men

plain_english: Why are they more powerful than you? Because they speak their useless words from real conviction. But you only speak your fancy words with your lips — that's why your words have no strength and are dead. It's sickening to listen to your preaching and your pathetic virtue that gets talked about everywhere. This is how ordinary people have the upper hand over you. Every real belief is strong and unshakeable. Until good thoughts are truly fixed in you, and you've built real strength to protect yourself, I advise you to be careful around common people. If you're not careful, whatever you write on your mind in school will melt away every day like wax in the sun.
original_excerpt: Why then are they more powerful than you? Because they utter these useless words from their real opinions; but you utter your elegant words only from your lips; for this reason they are without strength and dead, and it is nauseous to listen to your exhortations and your miserable virtue, which is talked of everywhere (up and down). In this way the vulgar have the advantage over you; for every opinion ([Greek: dogma]) is strong and invincible. Until then the good ([Greek: chompsai]) sentiments ([Greek: hupolaepseis]) are fixed in you, and you shall have acquired a certain power for your security, I advise you to be careful in your association with common persons; if you are not, every day like wax in the sun there will be melted away whatever you inscribe on your minds in the school.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought with Caution to Enter into Familiar Intercourse with Men

plain_english: Stay away from temptation while your resolve is still weak, like wax that melts in the sun. This is why philosophers tell people to leave their home country. Old habits distract you and prevent you from building new ones. You also can't stand people who see you and say, 'Look, there's so-and-so trying to be a philosopher now.' Doctors do the same thing — they send patients with chronic illnesses to different places with different air. And they're right to do it. You should do this too. Build new habits to replace your old ones. Set your beliefs and practice them.
original_excerpt: Withdraw then yourselves far from the sun so long as you have these waxen sentiments. For this reason also philosophers advise men to leave their native country, because ancient habits distract them and do not allow a beginning to be made of a different habit; nor can we tolerate those who meet us and say: See such a one is now a philosopher, who was once so and so. Thus also physicians send those who have lingering diseases to a different country and a different air; and they do right. Do you also introduce other habits than those which you have; fix you opinions and exercise yourselves in them.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought with Caution to Enter into Familiar Intercourse with Men

plain_english: But you don't do this. Instead, you go off to watch a show or gladiators or athletes or the circus. Then you come back here. Then you go back to those places again. Always the same people doing the same things. You never develop good habits. You never pay attention or take care of yourself or watch what you're doing. You never ask: How should I handle what happens to me? Should I respond naturally or unnaturally? Am I reacting the right way or the wrong way? Do I tell myself that things outside my control don't concern me? If you're not doing this yet, run from your old habits. Get away from ordinary people if you ever want to become something worthwhile.
original_excerpt: But you do not so; you go hence to a spectacle, to a show of gladiators, to a place of exercise ([Greek: chuston]), to a circus; then you come back hither, and again from this place you go to those places, and still the same persons. And there is no pleasing (good) habit, nor attention, nor care about self and observation of this kind. How shall I use the appearances presented to me? according to nature, or contrary to nature? how do I answer to them? as I ought, or as I ought not? Do I say to those things which are independent of the will, that they do not concern me? For if you are not yet in this state, fly from your former habits, fly from the common sort, if you intend ever to begin to be something.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought with Caution to Enter into Familiar Intercourse with Men

plain_english: When you complain that life is unfair, stop and think. You'll see that things happen for good reasons. 'But the dishonest person gets ahead!' In what way? In money? Sure, because they're better than you at flattering people, having no shame, and staying alert to opportunities. So what? But check if they beat you at being trustworthy or decent. You won't find that they do. Where you're actually superior, that's where you have the real advantage. I once asked a man who was bitter about Philostorgus's success: Would you want to sleep with Sura?
original_excerpt: ON PROVIDENCE.-When you make any charge against Providence, consider, and you will learn that the thing has happened according to reason. Yes, but the unjust man has the advantage. In what? In money. Yes, for he is superior to you in this, that he flatters, is free from shame, and is watchful. What is the wonder? But see if he has the advantage over you in being faithful, in being modest; for you will not find it to be so; but wherein you are superior, there you will find that you have the advantage. And I once said to a man who was vexed because Philostorgus was fortunate: Would you choose to lie with Sura?
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought with Caution to Enter into Familiar Intercourse with Men

plain_english: "May that day never come," he said. Then why are you upset if he gets something back for what he's selling? How can you think someone is happy when they get things through methods you hate? What's wrong with Providence giving better things to better people? Isn't it better to be modest than to be rich? He agreed it was. Then why are you upset when you have the better thing? Always remember this truth and keep it ready: it's a law of nature that whoever is superior has an advantage in the area where they're superior. Remember this and you'll never be upset.
original_excerpt: May it never happen, he replied, that this day should come? Why then are you vexed, if he receives something in return for that which he sells; or how can you consider him happy who acquires those things by such means as you abominate; or what wrong does Providence, if he gives the better things to the better men? Is it not better to be modest than to be rich? He admitted this. Why are you vexed then, man, when you possess the better thing? Remember then always and have in readiness the truth, that this is a law of nature, that the superior has an advantage over the inferior in that in which he is superior; and you will never be vexed.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought with Caution to Enter into Familiar Intercourse with Men

plain_english: But my wife treats me badly. Well, if someone asks you what this is, say: my wife treats me badly. Is there anything more to it? No. My father gives me nothing. What is this? My father gives me nothing. Is there anything else? No. But calling this an evil — that's something you add on top of it. And you add it wrongly. This is why we shouldn't try to get rid of poverty. We should get rid of our opinions about poverty. Then we'll be happy.
original_excerpt: But my wife treats me badly. Well, if any man asks you what this is, say, my wife treats me badly. Is there then nothing more? Nothing. My father gives me nothing. (What is this? my father gives me nothing. Is there nothing else then? Nothing); but to say that this is an evil is something which must be added to it externally, and falsely added. For this reason we must not get rid of poverty, but of the opinion about poverty, and then we shall be happy.
source_reference: Discourses, That We Ought with Caution to Enter into Familiar Intercourse with Men
